claims.claim: ISCED 2011 defines education as the processes by which societies deliberately transmit accumulated information, knowledge, understanding, attitudes, values, skills, competencies and behaviours across generations, involving communication designed to bring about learning.

ISCED 2011 defines learning as the individual acquisition or modification of information, knowledge, understanding, attitudes, values, skills, competencies or behaviours through experience, practice, study or instruction — an individual-level change, distinct from the organized activity intended to produce it.

In ISCED 2011, formal education is education that is institutionalised, intentional and planned through public organizations and recognised private bodies which in their totality constitute a country's formal education system; its qualifications are by definition recognised by the relevant national education authorities.

In ISCED 2011, non-formal education is also institutionalised, intentional and planned by an education provider, but functions as an addition, alternative or complement to formal education within lifelong learning; it is typically delivered as short courses, workshops or seminars and mostly leads to qualifications that national authorities do not recognise as formal or equivalent, or to no qualification at all.

ISCED 2011 defines informal learning as forms of learning that are intentional or deliberate but not institutionalised, occurring in the family, workplace, local community and daily life; it explicitly distinguishes informal learning from incidental or random learning, which is not organized or involves communication not designed to bring about learning and which ISCED excludes.

Programmes delivered partly in the workplace, such as apprenticeships, can count as formal education when they lead to a qualification recognised by national education authorities, so the formal/non-formal boundary tracks institutional recognition rather than physical location.

ISCED 2011 counts recognised qualifications toward educational attainment however they were obtained, including through non-formal education or informal learning, and explicitly allows classification of qualifications awarded through validation of prior learning.

ISCED 2011 remains the current version of the classification, maintained by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics as custodian, alongside ISCED-F 2013 (fields) and ISCED-T 2021 (teacher training); it was adopted by the UNESCO General Conference in November 2011 and published in 2012.

Sustainable Development Goal 4 is worded as ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and promoting lifelong learning opportunities for all, with targets covering technical and vocational education, adult skills, and youth and adult literacy.

The UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning describes lifelong learning as covering learners of all ages, all life-wide contexts (family, school, community, workplace), and formal, non-formal and informal modalities, and stresses recognition, validation and accreditation of skills gained non-formally or informally.

Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) states that everyone has the right to education, that education shall be free at least in the elementary and fundamental stages, that elementary education shall be compulsory, and that education shall be directed to the full development of the human personality and to strengthening respect for human rights.

Article 13 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights turns the right to education into treaty obligations: primary education compulsory and free to all; secondary education generally available and accessible with progressive introduction of free education; higher education equally accessible on the basis of capacity; and fundamental education encouraged for those who did not complete primary education.
UNESCO reports that 155 countries legally guarantee nine or more years of compulsory education while only 99 countries legally guarantee at least twelve years of free education.

UNESCO's out-of-school dashboard reports that as of 2024 roughly 273 million children and youth were out of school worldwide (about 79 million of primary age, 64 million of lower secondary age and 130 million of upper secondary age), so the normative right coexists with large unmet provision.

Sociologists dispute what education does and should do: functionalist accounts name manifest functions such as socialization, social control, social placement, cultural transmission and sorting, while conflict-theory accounts emphasise cultural capital, the hidden curriculum and tracking as mechanisms that reproduce inequality.

Terminology differs by discipline: sociology textbooks often use 'informal education' for learning cultural values and norms through participation in society, whereas ISCED reserves 'informal learning' for intentional but non-institutionalised learning and treats unplanned acquisition as incidental or random learning.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the third category should be called 'informal education' or 'informal learning', and whether it includes unintentional learning.
positions: ISCED 2011 (UNESCO-UIS): 'informal learning' is intentional or deliberate but not institutionalised; unplanned acquisition is a separate excluded category called incidental or random learning.

General sociology usage (e.g. OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e): 'informal education' covers learning cultural values, norms and expected behaviours by participating in society, without insisting on intentionality.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the ISCED terminology as the statistical standard, names the intentionality criterion explicitly, and flags that other disciplines use 'informal education' more loosely. Neither usage is presented as an error; the lesson tells learners to state which framework they are using.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether education's purposes can be settled empirically.
positions: Functionalist accounts describe education as performing socialization, sorting and cultural transmission functions for society.
Conflict accounts argue those same mechanisms reproduce existing inequality through the hidden curriculum, tracking and cultural capital.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson separates the empirical dispute (what schooling actually does) from the normative dispute (what it ought to do) rather than declaring a winner, and cites the sociological perspectives as evidence that the dispute exists.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The earlier draft treated 'informal education' as a settled third ISCED-style category and implied it means unstructured everyday learning; ISCED 2011 defines informal *learning* as intentional but non-institutionalised and separates it from incidental or random learning.

The earlier draft's common-mistake entry framed informal learning as something people wrongly call 'accidental', without stating that ISCED does recognise an accidental category (incidental or random learning) and excludes it from education statistics.

The earlier draft classified 'job-based practice' as informal learning and a self-paced tutorial as merely 'structured self-directed learning' without applying the institutionalisation and recognition criteria that actually decide ISCED classification.

The earlier draft attributed a general 'UNESCO describes education as including formal instruction as well as nonformal and informal learning' framing without identifying the instrument (ISCED 2011) or its criteria.
The earlier draft cited a source id for an OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 2e page and a generic UNESCO query-list URL; neither was verified for this lesson.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced 'informal education' with ISCED's 'informal learning' and added the excluded category of incidental or random learning.
Anchored all three category definitions in ISCED 2011's actual criteria (institutionalised, intentional, planned; recognition of qualifications) rather than in loose descriptions of setting.
Added that apprenticeships and other partly workplace-based programmes can be formal education when they lead to a recognised qualification.
Added that recognised qualifications count toward attainment however obtained, including through validation of prior non-formal or informal learning.
Made the descriptive/normative distinction concrete with the UDHR/ICESCR texts on one side and the 2024 out-of-school figures and country counts of legal guarantees on the other.
Grounded the 'purposes are contested' claim in named sociological positions instead of asserting contestation without evidence.
Expanded from 3 questions to a 5-item bank with difficulty, skill and source tagging, and added the required analogy limits.
Verified live that ISCED 2011 is still the current classification and that UIS is its custodian.
rightsIssues: ISCED 2011 (UNESCO-UIS, 2012, ISBN 978-92-9189-123-8) carries no explicit open licence that could be verified; treated as REFERENCE_ONLY. Only short attributed definitional phrases are quoted; no passage is adapted or reproduced at length.

The UNESCO Institute for Statistics site reorganised its URLs; the ISCED 2011 PDF is no longer served from the old uis.unesco.org/sites/default/files path. The canonical UNESDOC record is cited, and the live UIS methods-and-tools page is cited alongside it as a fetchable confirmation.

UNESDOC and OHCHR HTML pages return HTTP 403 to automated fetchers. The ICESCR text was verified from OHCHR's own PDF (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/cescr.pdf, HTTP 200) and the ISCED text from the published PDF of the same UNESCO-UIS document.

OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e is published under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 as stated on the book pages. Because the project's commercial status is not established here, it is recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY and no OpenStax wording is reused.
